brief.head: Firms make the nation
brief.text: A rich country is made of sophisticated firms, Ajay Shah said. Policy can only set the conditions; the real change lies in the culture of India’s elite. {034-C11}

brief.head: Options for the boss
brief.text: A salaried CEO stays wary of risk, Ajay Shah said. Stock options give a strong upside: if the firm grows 5x or 10x, the CEO benefits big time. {#stockoptions}

brief.head: Execution as comfort
brief.text: Indian managements retreat into execution, Ajay Shah said, because strategy means facing an unpredictable world and making difficult calls. Boards and advisors should pull them out. {034-C09}

brief.head: Lost in a generation
brief.text: When a family becomes wealthy, Amit Varma said, about 70 per cent of that wealth is lost by the next generation, and 90 per cent by the one after. {034-C10}

brief.head: Exam-topper worship
brief.text: Ajay Shah mocked India’s reverence for exam toppers: “the instinctive respect that somebody who could solve maths problems in 12th standard is a cool guy”. {034-J03}

thought.text: The only way to build a great business is to roll the dice
thought.who: Ajay Shah, arguing that founders with everything in one firm become too timid

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s masterclass on the four designs of a firm
lead.head: Blame the design, not the family
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, business has a caste system. People look down on traditional business families and revere the professional who passed an IIT entrance exam.
Shah called this the wrong way to think about the world. “We should think about incentives,” he said, “we should think about the forces that create good and bad decisions inside firms.” {034-C01}
To prove it, he built a firm on air: Amitbhai Media Limited, owned and run, at first, by Amit Varma.
Each design was judged on the same questions. Are the owners and the managers aligned? Will the people in charge take risks? And how concentrated is power?
## Four ways to run a firm
In Design One, Varma owns 100 per cent and is CEO. Alignment is perfect, but with most of his wealth in one firm, he will be too timid to take big bets.
Nobody can tell him no, either. “In this firm, you are the little deity,” Shah said. {034-C02}

Design Two sells 40 per cent to outsiders, perhaps through an IPO. It is common among listed Indian family firms, Shah said, and changes little: the founder stays cautious and unchallenged, and can now take more than his share of the cash.
Design Three is the one the Indian elite applauds. The family steps aside and hires a professional CEO on a salary, with no equity. Shah was unimpressed.

With no skin in the game, he said, the CEO spends the first three years trying not to be sacked and the rest coasting, while quietly gathering power. An IIT degree, Shah said, “doesn’t change things. It’s an incentives question.” {034-C05}
“We made it worse with design two, and we made it even worse with design three,” Varma said, and pleaded: “And now we need to get to design four, please save Amitbhai Media Limited.”
## The board takes charge

Design Four, Shah said, is how large firms work all over the world. There is no promoter. Shares are spread among institutions and the public, something that has begun in India only in the last 10 or 15 years.

Shareholders choose a board of about seven: the CEO, roughly three directors whose stakes matter to them, and roughly three independents. It sets strategy and organisation design, hires the CEO and holds the CEO to account. {034-C06}
Sometimes the board makes life too hot for the CEO, who leaves. Shah called that healthy.
None of this can be written into law, he stressed. It is culture, and it takes decades.
## The road from here
Varma asked how a real family firm should make the journey, since it cannot reach Design Four overnight.

If someone in the family has the hunger, Shah said, a family-led path beats hiring a professional. Power with an aligned family member is relatively safe; power with an unchecked hired manager is the worry. So build the board first, and only then bring in the outsider. {034-C08}
That asks the incumbent CEO to give up power, which is rare. Shah has sat on more than 20 boards and has seen, he said, “just disgusting levels of arrogance”.
Both hosts closed with family sagas: Shah with Thomas J Watson Jr’s IBM memoir, *Father, Son & Co*, and Varma with *The Godfather*, book and films.

second.label: Firms of one
second.head: Talking to the mirror
second.deck: Amit Varma finds his own career in Design One, flaws and all
body: Listening to Ajay Shah describe a firm whose founder owns all of it and runs it, Amit Varma recognised himself. Every creator, he said, is an entrepreneur of his own brand, at once shareholder and CEO. {034-S03}

He likened himself to Travis Bickle talking to the mirror in *Taxi Driver*, then added: “I can’t act, of course.” {034-J07} The upside is alignment. He follows his own vision, and has passed up great opportunities to do the things he loves.

The cost is scale, and the limits of his own imagination and knowledge. Shah added that employees would not change that. “If you have employees, they don’t readily challenge you enough because you’re 100%.” {#challenge}

quote.text: I think of every creator as being an entrepreneur of his own brand.

second.caption: being a firm of one

third.head: Even Jobs got it wrong
body: The business world loves a visionary. It credits a firm’s success to a great CEO and blames failure on a bad one. Ajay Shah thinks this attribution is “profoundly wrong”.

Much of the outcome, he said, is dumb luck: being in the right industry at the right time, or the world suddenly changing. Steve Jobs, the business world’s favourite visionary, made many wrong decisions. “He almost took Apple into bankruptcy,” Shah said. {034-J08}
The world is infinitely complicated, and no strong CEO understands it. “It is only by harnessing many, many minds that we have a hope of understanding the world better,” he said. {034-C07}
When power is concentrated in one person, he added, the quality of decisions is generally inferior. Indian business, he said later, is still stuck in a “primitive great man theory”. {#greatman}
third.caption: the great-man myth

p2.title: The firm, four ways
p2.deck: Ajay Shah builds Amitbhai Media Limited four times, and Amit Varma begs him to save it. {034-J02}

sections.label: Design One
sections.head: One owner, no arguments
sections.caption: the founder who owns it all
body: Start with the simplest firm. Amit Varma owns 100 per cent of Amitbhai Media Limited and is also its CEO. There are many such firms all around us in India, Ajay Shah said.
What goes right is alignment. The interests of the firm, the CEO and the shareholder are one, and the owner will run hard.

What goes wrong is risk. With too much of the owner’s wealth in one firm, he becomes cautious and invests only in small, incremental steps. Yet capitalism needs earth-shaking gambles, Shah said: some firms succeed outrageously, many die, “and that’s a good thing”. {034-C03}

Timid firms are not repositioned for the next wave of markets and technology, and are rendered irrelevant as the years go by. The flaw, Shah said, is not that the person is a bad one. It is the stance on risk.
## Nobody to say no

The second difficulty is concentrated power. With no check and balance, and nobody to force arguments before decisions, bad decisions are made, money is wasted and wrong projects are taken up. {034-C02}
Hiring staff would not fix it, he added. Employees rarely challenge someone who owns 100 per cent.
~ Many people start with this design, Shah said, and hopefully evolve out of it into a better firm.

quote.text: In this firm, you are the little deity, you are the God, you do all the thinking, you make all the decisions.

sections.label: Design Two
sections.head: Same boss, new partners
sections.caption: selling 40 per cent to outsiders
body: In Design Two, Amit Varma keeps 60 per cent and stays CEO, while two minority shareholders, Vaishnav and Nomsita, take 20 per cent each. It may even be a listed company. Ajay Shah said this is a very common design among Indian family firms.

Alignment stays high. The founder is slightly more diversified, but 60 per cent of the firm is still likely to be the biggest thing on his balance sheet, and his ego and standing are bound up in it. So he stays risk-averse. {#ego}
Power is as concentrated as before. The 40 per cent have none.
## A new problem
Particularly in India, Shah said, a 60 per cent owner can extract more than 60 per cent of the cash. {#extract} Investors who expect less than their share will pay less for the shares.

Most of India’s company law and SEBI rules for listed firms fight this one battle, he said. It is a fair question, but the debate has missed the bigger flaws: an under-diversified owner with excessive power. {034-C04}
~ “You are unshakable,” Shah told Varma. “There is no debate, there is no discussion.”

quote.text: This is the one question that has occupied the Indian imagination.

sections.label: Design Three
sections.head: The CEO with no skin
sections.caption: the salaried professional CEO
body: Design Three, Ajay Shah said, is the one loved by the Indian elite. Amit Varma keeps 60 per cent but steps aside, and a so-called professional from IIT is hired as CEO, on a salary and with no equity.
Varma reminded “gentle readers” that Shah is himself from IIT. “This is most insidious,” he said, “but continue.” {034-J04}
The new CEO has no skin in the game. Hired for a five-year term, the professional thinks: “The one thing I don’t want is to be sacked at the end of three years.” {#sacked}
So the first three years go on cost control and incremental improvements. Then the CEO squeaks through to a second term, and coasts to ten years without rocking the boat.
## Same problems, plus one

The chairman, who hires the CEO and can fire them, keeps nudging them away from risk, and is unlikely to be stopped from taking extra cash. And the CEO consolidates power inside the firm, with nobody to question them. {#powercorrupts}
~ If the family steps back in, the gossip columns say the professional is not in charge. “Either way, it’s a mug’s game,” Shah said.

quote.text: You’ve given power to a person without skin and it works pretty badly.

sections.label: Design Four
sections.head: Seven people in a room
sections.caption: the board that runs the firm
body: Design Four is how large, complex firms work all over the world, Ajay Shah said. There is no promoter. Shares are spread among institutions and the public, and that has begun in India only in the last 10 or 15 years. {#dispersed}
The shareholders pick a board. On a good one sit the CEO, about three shareholder directors whose 5 to 15 per cent stakes matter to them, and about three independent directors.
The board debates and approves the firm’s strategy and its organisation design. {034-C06} It hires the CEO and controls the CEO’s pay.
## Heat in the boardroom
“Why are we not winning? Why is our competitor doing better?” the board asks. Sometimes it is too hot for the CEO, who leaves, and Shah called that good and healthy. {#toohot}

Stock options give the CEO a strong upside, and diversified shareholders can accept that some firms will fail. When what sounded like a cat screamed in the background, Amit Varma explained it as “a CEO who had been ejected by the animal behaviour of an unruly board”. {034-J05}
~ None of this can be codified in laws, Shah stressed. It is culture, and it takes decades for a country to evolve to this kind of power relationship.

quote.text: But the strategy of the firm is controlled by the board, where the CEO is a member.

sections.label: Getting there
sections.head: Build the board first
sections.caption: the road from family firm to Design Four
body: The leap from Design Three to Design Four, Amit Varma said, is far vaster than the steps before it. And making a fortune is no guarantee of keeping it: about 70 per cent of a family’s new wealth is lost by the next generation. {034-C10}
He thought of the Nehrus, who “got lesser and lesser as people”, and of the Ambanis. “Every Dhirubhai is not going to have a Mukesh,” he said. {034-J11}

Ajay Shah agreed that the professional is no panacea, and that family members are not bad people. Where the family has a successor with the hunger, he would favour a family-led path towards Design Four.
## The order of things
First spread the shareholding, he advised, and build the board as an institution, with three shareholder directors and three independents. Only then bring in the hired CEO. {034-C08}
Strategy advisors help too, by challenging managements that would rather stick to execution. “You go home and watch TV, you don’t have to think too much,” Shah said. {034-C09}
~ Some families have no choice. When venture capital and private equity investors exit after an IPO, Shah said, the firm ends up with dispersed shareholders and must make Design Four work. {#vc}

quote.text: When a family becomes wealthy, 70% of that wealth is lost by the next generation, 90% is lost by the generation after that.

side.boxText: Amit Varma cited a Harvard Business Review article, *What You Can Learn from Family Business*, and Ajay Shah agreed with everything in it. Professionally run firms do better in good times, it finds, but family firms do less badly in bad times. {034-R07}

contQuote.text: The story of India’s emergence from being a poor country to our dreams of becoming a rich country is entirely in the firms. A rich country is made of sophisticated firms. A poor country is made of bad firms.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A thank-you note, a help desk, an IBM gamble and a film class

stories.start: So I I was in Delhi recently, actually three months ago
stories.end: I immediately said, Yeah, yeah, that's very much the guy.
stories.caption: Uja Sharma’s thank-you
stories.kicker: A student’s message, two decades in the making
stories.head: The thank-you that took 20 years
body: Three months before the episode, Amit Varma was in Delhi, and one of his writing students, Uja Sharma, recorded a message for Ajay Shah on Varma’s phone. She insisted it be played on the show, so Varma played it live, to catch Shah’s reaction.

Around 2000 or 2001, Sharma was a final-year student at the College of Business Studies in Delhi University, doing a project on futures and options. Ninety per cent of her research material, she said, bore Shah’s name. {#ninety}
She emailed him, not expecting to hear back. He replied promptly, and on a video call, on whatever platform the day offered, they talked for more than an hour.
Shah explained how derivatives worked, how the policy was coming together and what the NSE was doing. She went back, she said, “a lot smarter”, and aced the subject.
The lesson outlasted the exam. Making time for young people, she said, had stayed with her. “Every time a young person reaches out to me, I make time for them now.” {034-S01}
Shah, watching, had no memory of any of it. He had, he said, done this a lot.

~ Varma was not surprised. It clearly happened, he said, and it was exactly the kind of thing Shah does, going out of his way to help people when he has no reason to. “I immediately said, yeah, yeah, that’s very much the guy.”
stories.why: A video call of an hour, two decades ago, made Sharma someone who makes time for the young. Small acts of intellectual generosity can shape a person for decades without the giver ever knowing, and get passed on.
stories.postscript: Shah answered with a story of his own, about how strangers’ emails turned him into a help desk.

stories.caption: becoming a help desk
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the emails that found him his calling
stories.head: A help desk by divine decree
body: In the late 1990s, Ajay Shah said, derivatives trading was on the rise in Indian finance. He taught seminars all over the country, and did tutorial-style conversations on television that were played over and over, twice a day. {#tv} Many people came to see him as the teacher of derivatives.
Then the emails started. Strangers described their plans and their problems, and asked him to fix them. At first he was taken aback: he was not going to debug other people’s work.
“But by the fifth email, I got the message that the good Lord had intended for me to be a help desk,” he said. {034-S02}
~ So he decided to discharge his dharma, and has faithfully replied to all of them ever since. He still tries to make time for PhD students and early-stage academics.
stories.why: When the same kind of request keeps arriving at your door, it may be telling you where you are most useful. Accepting that role, as Shah did, can quietly do a lot of public good.

stories.start: this is the son of the great Tom Watson, who was the founder
stories.end: what it means to build a great firm like IBM as a family business
stories.caption: Tom Watson Jr’s gamble
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s pick: a family-business memoir from IBM
stories.head: The son who bet the house
body: Thomas J Watson Jr inherited IBM from his father, its founder. When the son started out, Ajay Shah said, IBM was “a funny feudal company where every morning people woke up and sang the company anthem”.

The son bet on the world’s most expensive operating system project, OS/360. {034-S04} In inflation-adjusted dollars, Shah said, it cost more than the Manhattan Project, and Watson led IBM through it all.
Watson told the story in *Father, Son & Co*, which Shah read when he was young. It is a pure family-business book, he said, about Designs One and Two, and a beautifully written one.
~ Earlier in the episode, Shah had said that the only way to build a great business is to roll the dice, and that founders with everything riding on one firm rarely dare. {034-C03}

quote.text: And Tom Watson Jr, the son, rolled the dice on the world’s most expensive operating system project.

stories.start: So I have a sad story here. I suddenly remembered this.
stories.end: everything you talk about good corporate culture, it was right there in that
stories.caption: Shamin Desai’s film class
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s pick, and a memory from Channel V
stories.head: Coppola in the promos room
body: Between 1995 and 1997, Amit Varma worked at Channel V, his second job. {#channelv} A filmmaker there, Shamin Desai, who sadly died a few years ago, gathered a few people from the promos department for a little film appreciation session.
With a dinky little recorder, Desai gave a talk. Francis Ford Coppola, he explained, made *Rumblefish* at the same time as *The Outsiders*, with pretty much the same cast.
“And he said *Rumblefish* is a masterpiece, spoke all about it, and played it,” Varma recalled. There were just five or six of them in the room. {034-S05}

~ Varma called it a masterclass in film appreciation, and added *Rumblefish* to his picks, after *The Godfather*, book and films. Everything Ajay Shah says about good corporate culture, he said, “was right there in that room”.
stories.why: A senior colleague taking the time to teach juniors, Varma suggested, is what good corporate culture looks like. It is the same lesson as Shah’s help desk and Uja Sharma’s message: make time for the young.

quiz.q: What did Uja Sharma learn from Ajay Shah’s hour-long video call, beyond how derivatives work?
quiz.a: To make time for young people whenever they reach out to her.

quiz.q: In Design One, why does a founder who owns 100 per cent take too few risks?
quiz.a: Too much of their wealth is locked in one firm: they are under-diversified.

quiz.q: Which single problem, according to Shah, do most Indian company law and SEBI rules try to fix?
quiz.a: Making sure minority shareholders get their fair share of the firm’s cash.

quiz.q: Why does a salaried professional CEO spend the first three years of a five-year term playing safe?
quiz.a: Being sacked after three years would destroy their career, so they avoid risk.

quiz.q: On a Design Four board of about seven, who sits alongside the CEO?
quiz.a: Roughly three shareholder directors with meaningful stakes and three independent directors.

quiz.q: What did Tom Watson Jr bet IBM on, and how big was the bet?
quiz.a: OS/360, which in inflation-adjusted dollars cost more than the Manhattan Project.
